title: A "Studio" is better than a "Game" for AI roleplay (a fouder's experience)
author: Pastrugnozzo
selftext:
Hello!

I've been building a solo roleplaying studio for over two years now. It transitioned from a no revenue project to a full-fledged business.
> It's been a wild ride, really.

My idea was to share my whole experience. The psychology of a founder, the community management, the marketing, the coding, the scaling, the prototyping.
But as I was staring at the blank page, I realize i wouldn't even know where to start.

Instead, I'm sharing a bite-sized lesson I've learned to see how this sub responds.
> I really hope this is inspiring or helpful for someone :)

# My transition from game to studio
Tale Companion, my project, was originally intended as a game.
> The idea is simple: AI defines rules, the user plays by them.

We're talking back when GPT 3.5 Turbo was the flagship model. You can imagine the quality of the gameplay...
If you weren't around back then, imagine a fever dream. Of a schizo person. AI kept making mistakes. And since the idea was that of a game with rules, you couldn't go back and correct them.

But gameplay quality wasn't even the main issue. The main issue was what people *wanted*. And this, I think, is a lesson in finding the product-market fit.

I kept trying to build a game with rules because that was what I enjoyed building. Yet not even I enjoyed the gameplay experience.
Only one year later I asked myself the right question: "What would I enjoy playing?"
> Of course, I'm lucky to be my own customer avatar.

And the answer was a revelation to me. I didn't want the inventory systems, I didn't want the combat, I didn't want the rules or the HP tracking.
Over everything else, I wanted *control*. I wanted to define NPCs' personalities, cities, locations, history, religion. And then I wanted to see AI breathe life into all of that while I played.

Over time, the identity of the game completely changed. From struggling to make AI never wrong and enforcing its rules better, I transitioned to making the most customizable experience possible.
In the meantime, AI quality also skyrocketed. Models like Claude Opus 4.5 are devastating in terms of RP quality.

# What does a studio do?
I am proud of what Tale Companion can do for two reasons:
1. It has a great memory system. The learning curve might be steep, but it gives you total control. Plus, it's powerful enough so you can play for years on the same game save.
2. It is agentic. What does it mean? You can chat with more than one AI model at once in the same room. This is extremely powerful because you can offload tasks. Say an agent roleplays for a specific party character, while another updates the memory system in the background based on the main, big narrator AI's outputs.

And I've been building further, from a visual novel mode to audio engines for custom sounds. The cool thing is everything I build on top of this can leverage the agentic aspect. So now AI agents can change music or background as I travel.

My users love this, and every day more and more people come and stick. I am a player of my own game, which is flattering too. I couldn't be happier about this, and I can't wait to learn more.

And all of this couldn't have happened if I didn't escape my own mental jail. It's funny how many questions you don't even ask yourself whose answers would save your life.

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body: This reads like a stealth ad. But alright, I'll bite. What makes it different from any normal LLM based text RPG tool with embedded memory other than being admittedly kind of pretty?

replies.author: Flash1987
replies.body: Lol every post in this sub is an ad

replies.author: Pastrugnozzo
replies.body:
No I'm not just saying that the memory system runs in parallel.

I'm saying you can create and configure multiple agents in just one chat, then give them custom prompts and models.

One agent might roleplay as your party member, another one your game master, etc. This is cool to me because it lets you have any kind of game structure you can think of. From being the GM of many AI players to simple 1on1 sessions with a narrator.

Is this an ad? I don't know, it's me sharing an experience. If someone is interested in the game, cool. If someone is interested in the lessons I've learned, cool. I don't really care :)

comments.author: SproutsJeremy
comments.body:
Yeah what you’re saying makes a lot of sense. AI always makes mistakes after you spend a certain amount of time with a story due to context limitations. In order to get the perfect story there’s a lot of customization work that needs to be done behind the scenes to get what you want. So it’s best you put all the tools in the hands of the creator so they can create the perfect story for any story they want, and also create the perfect story for others in the community. 

This is a good post for people who are creating AI companion apps. More customizability means a far tighter more seamless experience.
